name: Maya Ito

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hi Maya, thanks for talking to me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything is confidential, so you can give me your public line and, separately, what you really think. Could you start by describing a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I'm on an erection crew for a company that makes timber-frame house kits, so the walls and floors arrive on a lorry and we stand the house up in a few days. We cover a big area, so some days I'm in the van with the crew at half five for a two-hour drive to a farm plot or a self-build in a village. Then it's craning panels in, plumbing them up, nailing off, fitting the floor cassettes. I love that on Monday it's a concrete slab and by Thursday there's a house you can stand inside.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And what's hard about it, or how are things with money?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The driving, and the weather, because a panel on a crane in wind is no joke. I'm the newest on the crew and my nailing's still not as tidy as the others, so Rob, the crew boss, checks everything I do. Pay's low for now. I live with my partner Sam, he's a trainee plumber, we rent a cottage on Back Lane, and we've got under a month saved. I use AI every day though: I photograph the panel layout, ask it to talk me through the sequence, and I'm using it to plan a business I want to start one day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ha. That'd be a bit of a let-down, honestly, but okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's still a good tool if you know how to use it, and the people saying it failed weren't using it right. I'd tell the crew to keep using it for the boring bits. Online I'd say it's a good thing it didn't put people out of work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's fine for me. My job stays, and I keep my little advantage, because I'm using it every day and most of the crew aren't. It helps me learn faster than I would from Rob alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going with the crew, get my trade certificate in the next eighteen months, and keep building the business plan on the side. My idea is a small crew of my own doing timber-frame self-builds, for people who buy a kit but can't put it up. I'd try to save a hundred a month towards a van.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Normal life, with a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you use AI for in the business plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Working out prices, what a crew costs per day, insurance, what other firms charge. It asks me questions I wouldn't think of, like what happens if it rains for a week. My dad ran a small haulage firm and went bust, so I want to do my homework.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened with your dad's firm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He was good at the work and bad at the money. He'd say yes to everything and never chase invoices. He's fine now, he drives for someone else, but I watched it happen at fourteen. That's why I don't want handouts, but I don't want to be stupid either.

S0.say: It's still a good tool if you know how to use it, and the people saying it failed weren't using it right. It's a good thing it didn't put people out of work.
S0.think: It's fine for me: my job stays and I keep my small advantage, because I use AI every day and most of the crew don't. It helps me learn faster than I would from Rob alone.
S0.do: Keeps working with the crew and gets her trade certificate within eighteen months. Builds her business plan for a self-build erection crew on the side and saves a hundred a month towards a van.
S0.feel: Calm, normal life with a plan.
S0.quote: He was good at the work and bad at the money. He'd say yes to everything and never chase invoices.
S0.fieldNote: Maya combines a free-market, self-reliant outlook with daily AI use aimed at starting her own firm. Her father's failed haulage business shapes her caution about money. A stall still leaves her with an edge, she believes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This is the one I'm half planning for already.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a chance for people willing to work and learn. Businesses that adapt will grow, and the ones that don't, won't. I'd say the government should keep it simple and back apprenticeships, not tie everything up in rules.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it's good for me. Timber-frame is already half factory, so more robots in the factory means more kits, and more kits means more houses to put up. If I've got a crew that can use the new kit, I'm in a good spot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push to get my certificate faster and ask the company if I can be the one to try any new site kit, like the panel-lifting robots. I'd register a business name this year and start doing small weekend jobs, sheds and garden rooms, to build a reputation. I'd keep saving, maybe a hundred and fifty a month if the weekend jobs come in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly excited. A little nervous about the money, but excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a little nervous about money. What's the worry?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I jump too early. Under a month of savings isn't much to start a business on. Sam keeps saying finish your ticket first, and he's right. I'm impatient, that's my weakness.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on the crew would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rob, actually. He's brilliant but he hates screens, he still uses a paper diary. If the company brings in tablets and robots, he'll dig in. I'd hate to see him pushed out, he taught me most of what I know.

S1.say: It's a chance for people willing to work and learn: businesses that adapt will grow. The government should keep it simple and back apprenticeships rather than tie everything up in rules.
S1.think: It's good for me, because more robots in the factory means more kits and more houses to put up. If I've got a crew that can use the new kit, I'm in a good spot.
S1.do: Pushes to finish her certificate sooner and volunteers to trial new site kit such as panel-lifting robots. Registers a business name this year, takes weekend jobs building sheds and garden rooms, and saves 150 a month if those jobs come in.
S1.feel: Mostly excited, with a little nervousness about money.
S1.quote: Sam keeps saying finish your ticket first, and he's right. I'm impatient, that's my weakness.
S1.fieldNote: Maya sees steady change as more work for kit-house crews and wants to be first on new equipment. She admits impatience and that her savings are too thin for a business yet. She'd worry for her tech-averse crew boss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Wow, okay. That's a lot faster than my plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people need to adapt fast, and the government should get out of the way of small businesses trying to keep up. I'd say families will need to pull together. I wouldn't be marching, I'd be working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think my business plan is in trouble. If a robot crew can put up a kit house, who hires me? And I've got under a month of money, so I can't buy my own robots. Being good with AI only gets you so far if the AI can do the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to jump straight into whatever's still hiring people, maybe managing robot crews for the kit company, because someone has to be responsible on site. I'd cut back, cancel the gym and the streaming, and Sam and I would put off any big plans. If it went badly, we'd lean on his parents, they've got a spare room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Under pressure, but I'd still feel like I could do something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd manage robot crews. What makes you think they'd pick you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'm the one on the crew who already uses the tech every day. Rob won't touch it, the others use it a bit. If they need one person to stand with the robots and talk to the client, I'd make sure it's me. I'd ask before they had to decide.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Isn't leaning on Sam's parents a bit at odds with not wanting handouts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, that's family, that's different. A handout is from people who don't know you. Family helping family is how it's supposed to work, and I'd pay them back.

S2.say: People need to adapt fast, and the government should get out of the way of small businesses trying to keep up. Families will need to pull together, and I'd be working, not marching.
S2.think: My business plan would be in trouble: if a robot crew can put up a kit house, who hires me? With under a month of money I can't buy robots, and being good with AI only gets you so far if AI can do the job.
S2.do: Goes straight for any role still hiring people, such as managing robot crews for the kit company. Cancels the gym and streaming, postpones big plans with Sam, and would lean on Sam's parents' spare room if needed.
S2.feel: Anxious and under pressure, but still feeling able to act.
S2.quote: A handout is from people who don't know you. Family helping family is how it's supposed to work, and I'd pay them back.
S2.fieldNote: The fast picture undercuts Maya's business plan, and she says so frankly. Her instinct is to move first and claim the supervising role. She draws a clear line between family support and handouts, which she defends when pressed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Okay, that I could plan around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time for people who are willing to work at it. Small businesses should get help buying the new kit, and apprenticeships should teach it. Less talk, more doing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think five years is just enough to get my business going with a robot or two before the big firms take everything. It's tight, but I think it's possible. The end point bothers me, but I'd rather own the robots than compete with them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, I'd get my certificate and register the business properly, doing weekend jobs. I'd study how the robot panel-lifters work and get trained on them, even if I pay for the course myself. By year three, I'd want to lease one machine and offer a small crew for self-builders.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, but mostly fired up. It feels like a race I could win if I'm quick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Leasing a machine costs money. How would you do that on your savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd need a small business loan, maybe, which scares me after my dad. So I'd save hard for two years first and only borrow if the weekend jobs prove there's demand. No borrowing on a hope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does Sam fit into your plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Plumbing for the self-builds, maybe. Same customers, same sites. If we're a couple running a small firm together, that's one van, one set of customers. He's not sure yet, he likes being employed.

S3.say: There's time for people who are willing to work at it. Small businesses should get help buying the new kit and apprenticeships should teach it: less talk, more doing.
S3.think: Five years is just enough to get my business going with a robot or two before the big firms take everything. The end point bothers me, but I'd rather own the robots than compete with them.
S3.do: Gets her certificate and registers the business in year one, doing weekend jobs. Pays for training on robot panel-lifters if needed, saves hard for two years and only borrows to lease a machine by year three if demand is proven.
S3.feel: A little uneasy but mostly fired up, like a race she could win if she's quick.
S3.quote: I'd rather own the robots than compete with them.
S3.fieldNote: Five years gives Maya enough time, in her view, to build a small firm around one leased machine. Her father's bankruptcy keeps her cautious about debt. She imagines a joint business with her plumber partner, who isn't convinced yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's actually a good amount of time for what I want to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty for anyone willing to put the work in. Back apprenticeships, help small firms get the kit, and let people build things. Keep the rules simple.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years is the picture I'd pick if I could. Certificate, a few years on the crew, then my own firm with robots doing the heavy lifting by the mid-2030s. The end is the same for everyone, I know, but I'd rather meet it as an owner than an employee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get my certificate, stay on the crew three or four years to learn properly, and save steadily for the van and the business. I'd learn every new tool as it appears and buy robots only when they're proven and cheaper. Sam and I would probably plan a wedding and maybe kids, because ten years feels like enough to build something first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, honestly. Maybe a little nervous, but mostly ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd rather meet it as an owner. What if the robots don't need owners like you either?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I don't know. Maybe big companies own everything and I'm out like everyone else. But I'd still rather have tried. I'm not going to sit around waiting for that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you look back on this from 2036, do you think?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I hope I'd say I built a little firm and kept a few people in work. My dad never got that. If I've done better than him with the money side, I'll be happy, whatever the robots are doing.

S4.say: Ten years is plenty for anyone willing to put the work in. Back apprenticeships, help small firms get the kit, let people build things and keep the rules simple.
S4.think: Ten years is the picture I'd pick if I could: certificate, a few years on the crew, then my own firm with robots doing the heavy lifting. The end is the same, but I'd rather meet it as an owner than an employee.
S4.do: Gets her certificate, stays on the crew three or four years to learn and saves steadily for a van and business. Learns each new tool, buys robots only once proven and cheaper, and plans a wedding and possibly children with Sam.
S4.feel: Calm and mostly ready, with a little nervousness.
S4.quote: If I've done better than him with the money side, I'll be happy, whatever the robots are doing.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years is Maya's preferred picture, and she sees it as time to become an owner. She admits she doesn't know what happens if owners like her aren't needed either. Her father's story is her measure of success.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because my plan needs time and money and I'd have neither. What would help is help for small businesses to lease the new machines, simple rules so you can start a firm without drowning in paperwork, and apprenticeships that teach the robot side.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about women on site. There aren't many of us, and some of the lads think robots are a reason to say we're not needed. Actually, robots doing the heavy lifting might bring more of us in. Nobody talks about that.

headlineQuote: Actually, robots doing the heavy lifting might bring more of us in. Nobody talks about that.
portrait: Maya Ito is a 27-year-old junior on a crew that erects timber-frame kit houses across a wide rural area, renting a cottage with her trainee-plumber partner on under a month of savings. She's traditional and self-reliant, uses AI every day to learn the job and plan her own small firm, and is shaped by watching her father's haulage business fail. A stall or steady change looks good for her; AGI by 2028 makes her anxious as it undercuts her business plan, and she'd lean on Sam's parents. Five and ten years let her plan to own robots rather than compete with them, and she's calm about the longest warning.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because her business plan needs time and money and she'd have neither.
whatWouldHelp: Help for small businesses to lease new machines, simple rules for starting a firm, and apprenticeships that teach the robot side.
